name: Möckern

portrait.title: Eugène de Beauharnais, Viceroy of Italy

summary: Eugène, holding the Elbe with the remains of the Grande Armée and the first of the new conscript divisions, came out of Magdeburg towards Berlin and met Wittgenstein's Russians and Yorck's and Bülow's Prussians east of the river. It was three fights more than one battle: at Dannigkow, where Hünerbein's East Prussians stormed the village; at Vehlitz and the Windmühlenberg, where Borstell and Berg drove off the Italians; and at Zeddenick, where Oppen's cavalry routed the French horse. That night Eugène fell back to Magdeburg, and next day behind the Elbe.

sources.label: Prussian Corps, Generallieutenant Yorck, April–May 1813 (Nafziger Collection 813DBJ)

forces.name: Lagrange's Division
forces.summary: Lauriston's leading division, posted round Wahlitz with its outposts forward in Dannigkow and Gommern. Hünerbein's East Prussians stormed Dannigkow in the early afternoon and the village was fought over for hours, the 134th's companies holding it until the French drew back on Gommern at dusk.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' French 1812 list, the nearest to 1813: there is no list for the army Napoleon raised after Russia, largely of conscripts and of battalions drawn from depots all over the Empire.
After Nafziger's return of 25 April, three weeks after the fight; Nafziger has no order of battle for Möckern itself.
Its battalions were mostly young conscripts of the classes of 1813 and 1814. They are rated as ordinary Line, as they fought: the list's Wavering or Morale 5 would suit those who broke more readily.
The Irish Legion (3rd Foreign Regiment), two battalions, is shown as Line.
Regimental guns were lost in Russia and not replaced, so the division has none.
The division's two foot batteries, where the list allows one, show as a historical departure.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.

forces.name: Zucchi's Italian Brigade
forces.summary: The Italians held Vehlitz with four battalions and four guns, and two more on the Windmühlenberg behind it. When Borstell's Prussians and Berg's Russians came on in the late afternoon they refused a summons to surrender and were driven off the hill at the bayonet.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' Italian 1812 list, the nearest to 1813.
After Nafziger's return of 25 April, three weeks after the fight; Nafziger has no order of battle for Möckern itself.
The accounts give the brigade four guns at Vehlitz: the division's Italian horse battery, shown as a half battery. With fewer units than the list wants for it, it shows as a historical departure.
Zucchi, a brigadier, commands the force, so he is its commander rather than its brigade's.
The brigade has no divisional commander: Gérard's French brigade (the 6th and 112th Line) wasn't engaged.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.

forces.name: The Light Cavalry at Zeddenick
forces.formation: 1st Light Cavalry Division, I Cavalry Corps
forces.summary: All the horse Eugène had left after Russia, about 1,200 sabres in the remnants of a dozen regiments, holding Zeddenick on the right. Late in the day Oppen's Prussian horse came up with Cossacks and a half battery and put them to flight, and a counter-charge at Vehlitz was broken by a volley and two squadrons of Prussian dragoons.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' French 1812 list, the nearest to 1813: there is no list for the army Napoleon raised after Russia, largely of conscripts and of battalions drawn from depots all over the Empire.
After Nafziger's return of 25 April, three weeks after the fight; Nafziger has no order of battle for Möckern itself.

The German account names the 7th Chevau-légers, 8th Hussars and a 9th lancer regiment (Polish, it says; Nafziger has the 9th Chevau-légers), with parts of four chasseur regiments, about 1,200 horse with one battery. Nafziger puts them in Bruyère's division; the account doesn't name the commander.
Each regiment was a few hundred men at most, so the lancers and hussars are Small and the chasseurs one combined regiment.
Cavalry without infantry shows as a historical departure.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.

forces.name: Roth's Advance Guard
forces.summary: The head of Berg's corps, which reached Vehlitz about four in the afternoon and joined Borstell's Prussians in the attack on the village and the Windmühlenberg, its Jäger and militia covering the left; the Grodno Hussars helped break the French cavalry's counter-charge.
notes: Built from A Clash of Eagles' Russian list, which covers 1812-15.
By the spring of 1813 Russian infantry regiments were down to a single field battalion each, the rest having gone back to recruit; each regiment is shown as its one battalion.

The German account names the 26th Jäger, the Olonetz-Vologda militia battalion and two battalions of Berg's corps at Vehlitz, with the Grodno Hussars; the two battalions aren't named, so they are the 14th Division's Tenginsk and Estonia regiments, the 26th Jäger's own division, from Nafziger's order of battle for Lützen. So is the light battery.
The militia battalion is Opolchenie, attached to the Estonia regiment as the list takes it.
A Jäger brigade of one regiment, and a light battery with fewer battalions than the list wants for it, show as historical departures.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces; but 2 of the 3 brigade commanders at 7, as the list rates at most half of them higher.

forces.name: Yorck's Corps
forces.summary: The old Prussian auxiliary corps of 1812. Its advance guard under Hünerbein, three East Prussian battalions with hussars, dragoons, Cossacks and twelve guns, stormed Dannigkow and held it against Lagrange's counter-attacks; the rest of the corps stood at Leitzkau.
notes: Built from Albion Triumphant's Prussian 1815 list, the nearest to 1813: its Prussian Infantry Brigade is the 1813 brigade, the size of another army's division, with line, reserve and Landwehr battalions.
After Nafziger's returns for April; he has no order of battle for Möckern itself.
A Prussian brigade was the size of another army's division, so the whole corps is here. Take the brigades you want; each is a force in itself.

In the spring of 1813 the brigades had no Landwehr yet: each was two line regiments, with grenadier, reserve and Jäger battalions besides, so most have more line regiments, or more battalions in a regiment, than the list's brigade takes, which shows as historical departures.

Battalions of different regiments that served together are grouped as a regiment, as the list takes them. Reserve battalions are the list's Musketeers; grenadier battalions are Musketeers with its Veteran upgrade.
Brigades of three regiments or more have a Subordinate Commander, named where the order of battle names the brigade's infantry commander.
The Leib Regiment's fusilier battalion, a regiment of its own in Hünerbein's brigade, shows as a historical departure.

The brigades' cavalry is together as the corps cavalry: the Lithuanian Dragoons and the 2nd Leib Hussars' two halves from Hünerbein, the combined dragoons from Horn. The 2nd Combined Dragoons were two squadrons each of the 1st West Prussian and Brandenburg Dragoons.
The half 3-pdr battery is the list's Foot Artillery, as a half battery.

Batteries beyond the one each brigade takes are in the corps artillery, as the list's reserve takes them; more than it allows, or a reserve horse battery with fewer brigades than the list wants for it, show as historical departures.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.

forces.name: Bülow's Corps
forces.summary: Borstell's Pomeranian and East Prussian battalions, with the Queen's Dragoons, which took Vehlitz and the Windmühlenberg with Berg's Russians; and Oppen's cavalry, the 'mad' Major von Platen's dragoons and the Leib Hussars, which routed the French horse at Zeddenick.
notes: Built from Albion Triumphant's Prussian 1815 list, the nearest to 1813: its Prussian Infantry Brigade is the 1813 brigade, the size of another army's division, with line, reserve and Landwehr battalions.
After Nafziger's returns for April; he has no order of battle for Möckern itself.

Only Borstell's brigade and Oppen's cavalry fought at Möckern; Hesse-Homburg's and Clausewitz's brigades of Bülow's corps are left out. The Queen's Dragoons, Borstell's own, ride with Oppen's regiments here.

Battalions of different regiments that served together are grouped as a regiment, as the list takes them. Reserve battalions are the list's Musketeers; grenadier battalions are Musketeers with its Veteran upgrade.
Borstell's horse battery is in the corps artillery, as the list takes it.

In April 1813 the brigade had no Landwehr yet, which the list's brigade wants; that, Oppen's cavalry brigade with only one infantry brigade to allow it, and a reserve horse battery with too few brigades, show as historical departures.
Commanders are at Staff Rating 8, the default for historical forces.
